screens.title: Policy-Based Routing (PBR) and IP SLA
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how Policy-Based Routing lets you direct traffic using rules other than the normal destination-based lookup, and how IP SLA adds active measurements so those rules can respond to real-time path conditions. We'll ground the theory in common enterprise use cases: offloading application flows to a particular ISP, forcing traffic through a firewall, and implementing automatic failover when a primary link fails. You'll see the core building blocks: access lists to match traffic, route-maps to express actions, and IP SLA operations plus track objects to monitor reachability. A concrete example will walk through configuring a router with two internet paths and steering traffic from a subnet to the preferred next-hop, with IP SLA verifying availability and failing over to the backup. Also pay attention to the common mistakes: applying PBR on the wrong interface, misunderstanding directionality, or forgetting fallbacks. By the end you'll know not only how to write the commands, but how to test, verify, and reason about behavior under failure. Consider the question: when would you prefer PBR over policy in a routing protocol, and what monitoring interval would you choose for a business-critical application?

keyIdea.title: Why PBR + IP SLA matters
keyIdea.text: PBR gives fine-grained steering; IP SLA makes that steering adaptive. Together they enable predictable, resilient traffic paths for critical applications.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Policy-Based Routing & IP SLA
Policy-Based Routing (PBR) and IP SLA
Control traffic with policies and use active monitoring to make those policies resilient.

PBR lets you override normal routing by matching traffic with access lists and applying route-map actions. IP SLA actively tests a path and produces a tracked state that PBR can use to decide a next-hop.

You will practice configuring route-maps, ip policy, IP SLA operations, track objects, and the set ip next-hop verify-availability command that ties them together.

Visual Overview
Match
Access-lists identify traffic by source, proto, ports.
Act
Route-maps set next-hop, interface, or verify availability.
Monitor
IP SLA measures latency or reachability; track objects expose up/down state.
Concept Map
Three building blocks working together
Source-based steering
Send a subnet to an ISP of your choice regardless of destination.
Monitored failover
If primary next-hop fails, tracked IP SLA triggers the backup hop automatically.
Application steering
Force known application flows through security appliances when required.
Load sharing
Distribute different traffic classes across multiple uplinks for better utilization.
Explore Key Topics
PBR Basics
Match traffic and set next-hop using route-maps and access-lists.
IP SLA
Active probes measure reachability and performance of paths.
Integration
Use verify-availability with track objects to make failover automatic.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this first objectives page you will be able to explain when and why Policy-Based Routing is useful, and you will be able to configure PBR to forward traffic based on criteria other than destination. Specifically, you will learn how access lists define the traffic to match and how route-maps express the forwarding action. You'll see examples where source-based steering sends a subnet to a particular next-hop to meet business policy, and we'll contrast that with standard routing so you can predict effects on return paths. You'll also begin to configure IP SLA operations to monitor reachability, including choosing an appropriate test type like ICMP echo for simple reachability checks or TCP connect for service-aware monitoring. Each objective focuses on practical configuration and why the step matters in real networks. Pay attention to directionality: PBR applies to traffic entering an interface, which is a frequent source of mistakes. As you work through the lab steps, ask: which traffic should be matched, and how will return traffic behave once we force a specific next-hop?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: On this second page of objectives we focus on the integration, verification, and operational best practices that make PBR and IP SLA production-ready. You will implement IP SLA tracking and tie tracked state to route-map actions using the set ip next-hop verify-availability command so policy decisions depend on measured reachability. You will learn verification and troubleshooting commands—show ip policy, show ip sla summary, show track, and show ip cef exact-route—to confirm behavior and to observe how traffic moves under normal and failure conditions. Safety and operational notes are also objectives: choose reasonable IP SLA frequencies to avoid excessive control-plane traffic and always provide a fallback next-hop or allow the routing table to take over to avoid black holes. Lastly, you'll practice a hands-on scenario that configures R1 with both primary and secondary next-hops, exercises failover by shutting down an interface, and observes track state change. These are the operational skills that let you deploy PBR+IP SLA with confidence in a live network.

screens.title: What is Policy-Based Routing (PBR)?
screens.narratorSegment: Policy-Based Routing is a method to forward packets according to rules you define, instead of relying exclusively on the routing table's destination-based decision. In practice, you match traffic — often using an access list — and then set a forwarding action in a route-map. The motivation is straightforward: enterprise networks often need traffic steering that reflects business needs rather than pure topology. For example, you might force all voice traffic through a low-latency WAN link, or route traffic from a particular branch through a security appliance for inspection. PBR is also used for load sharing between two internet providers by steering different subnets to different next-hops. A common misconception is that PBR changes how return traffic is routed; it only affects the router where the policy is evaluated. That makes thinking about symmetric flows important: if you force outbound traffic to a different path, the return path might not return via the same device unless you design the network for it. As a takeaway, PBR is powerful for granular control, but you must plan matching criteria, return path symmetry, and fallbacks to avoid creating black holes.

keyIdea.title: PBR in one line
keyIdea.text: PBR overrides normal next-hop selection for matched traffic so you can implement source- or application-based steering.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › What is PBR?
Definition
Policy-Based Routing forwards packets based on matching criteria other than destination, such as source IP, application protocol, or port.
Key characteristics
  • Matches traffic with ACLs or other selectors.
  • Route-maps express actions like set ip next-hop or set interface.
  • Applied inbound on the interface where traffic enters the router.
Common misconception
PBR does not automatically affect traffic the router originates. To affect locally-generated traffic you must use local policy configuration.
Enterprise use cases
Force critical application through a secure firewall for inspection.
Steer voice or video over a low-latency path to meet QoS goals.
Load-share subnets across multiple ISPs.
Direct legacy app traffic through a specific service chain.
Concrete example
Match traffic from 192.168.10.0/24 and set the next-hop to 10.0.0.2 so that that subnet uses the primary ISP while all other traffic follows the routing table.
Key Takeaway
Use PBR for precise steering, but always include fallbacks and plan for asymmetric return paths.

screens.title: PBR building blocks: match, route-map, set action
screens.narratorSegment: PBR configuration follows a disciplined process with four core steps, and understanding each step helps you design safe policies. Step one is defining what traffic to match, typically with a standard or extended access-list that identifies source subnets, destination networks, protocol type, or ports. Step two is creating a route-map entry that uses match ip address to reference that access-list. Step three is defining the action with set commands: set ip next-hop to select a specific next-hop IP, or set interface to send traffic out a chosen interface. There is also verify-availability to consult a track object from IP SLA. The final step is applying the route-map to an ingress interface using ip policy route-map. A common error is applying the policy to the wrong interface or in the wrong direction; the router evaluates PBR only on traffic entering the interface where you applied the policy. Another important operational point is the order of set commands in a route-map: when you include verify-availability the router uses the tracked state to decide whether that set is valid and then falls through to subsequent sets. As an exercise, write the access-list, reference it from a route-map with permit 10, and apply ip policy on the client-facing interface. This disciplined sequence reduces misconfiguration and makes troubleshooting straightforward.

keyIdea.title: Four-step configuration
keyIdea.text: Match traffic with ACLs, create route-map entries, set forwarding behavior, and apply the route-map inbound on the ingress interface.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › PBR Building Blocks
Step-by-step
1. Define match
Create an ACL that matches the traffic you want to steer, for example source 192.168.10.0/24.
2. Create route-map
Use route-map NAME permit 10 and reference the ACL with match ip address 101.
3. Define action
Use set ip next-hop or set interface. Optionally use verify-availability with a track object for monitored failover.
4. Apply policy
Apply with ip policy route-map NAME on the ingress interface so traffic is evaluated as it arrives.
Example callouts
match ip address 101 — references the ACL you created to select traffic.
set ip next-hop 10.0.0.2 — forces chosen traffic to that next-hop.
ip policy route-map PBR_PRIMARY — attaches the policy to the interface handling client traffic.
Common pitfall
Applying PBR to the egress interface or applying it in the outbound direction is incorrect. The policy must be evaluated where traffic enters. Remember to consider traffic sourced by the router itself and use local policy if you need to catch that traffic.

screens.title: PBR vs. Normal Routing
screens.narratorSegment: Normal routing uses destination IP and the longest-prefix match rule to choose the outgoing interface and next-hop. That model is simple, scalable, and works for the vast majority of traffic. Policy-Based Routing is an intentional exception to that model: you introduce business-driven rules that can override the routing table for selected flows. Use PBR when you need deterministic steering based on source, protocol, or application rather than the destination. A classic use case is sending a subnet to a specific ISP for contractual or performance reasons, or directing application traffic through a security appliance for inspection. However, PBR adds operational complexity: policies are processed before the normal route lookup completes, and they only affect traffic processed by the router where the policy is applied. A common misunderstanding is to assume PBR will rewrite return traffic paths; in reality, PBR affects only the router performing the match. If two devices apply asymmetric PBRs you can create forwarding loops or drops, so test for symmetry and include fallback behaviors. In general, reserve PBR for flows that need special handling and prefer routing protocol solutions for broad reachability and dynamic path selection unless policy-level steering is required.

keyIdea.text: PBR is for policy-driven steering; normal routing should remain the default for general connectivity unless policy constraints demand otherwise.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › PBR vs Normal Routing
Normal Routing
  • Destination-based longest-prefix match.
  • Scales well for general traffic.
  • Uses routing protocols to determine best path.
When to prefer
General connectivity, large-scale dynamic path selection using routing protocols.
Policy-Based Routing
  • Match by source, protocol, or port and set forwarding action.
  • Applied inbound on a router interface to override routing table for matched traffic.
  • Enables application or contract-driven steering.
When to prefer
Specific traffic classes need deterministic forwarding regardless of routing metrics.
Misconception check
PBR does not alter how peers route back to you; it only influences forwarding on the router executing the policy. Always evaluate return-path symmetry and include fallbacks to the routing table.

screens.title: Common PBR Mistakes and Pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: Several mistakes recur when engineers implement PBR, and anticipating them saves time in deployment. First, applying the route-map on the wrong interface or in the wrong direction is the most common error. Remember, ip policy route-map is evaluated on traffic entering the interface, so apply it on the interface facing the traffic source. Second, administrators forget that PBR does not affect traffic the router itself originates; locally-generated packets are not evaluated by an interface policy unless you configure ip local policy route-map. Third, missing fallbacks can create black holes. Always include a secondary set ip next-hop or allow the route-map to fall through so the routing table can handle traffic if policy paths fail. Fourth, order matters: verify-availability is evaluated in the order of set statements in the route-map; if the verified next-hop is down, PBR falls through to the next set. Finally, excessive IP SLA frequency can overload control plane processing. Use conservative frequencies and balance detection speed with stability. When troubleshooting, show ip policy and show track will quickly reveal whether the policy is applied and whether the tracked object is up or down. Ask yourself: have I accounted for the router's locally-originated traffic and provided safe fallbacks?

keyIdea.text: Apply PBR inbound on the correct interface, handle local traffic explicitly, include fallbacks, and choose appropriate IP SLA intervals.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Common PBR Mistakes
Top pitfalls
  • Applying policy on the wrong interface or in the outbound direction.
  • Neglecting locally-originated traffic — use ip local policy when needed.
  • No fallback next-hop or route table fallback leads to black holes.
  • Misordered set statements when using verify-availability.
  • Aggressive IP SLA frequency causing control-plane load.
Troubleshooting checklist
1. Confirm policy is applied: show ip policy.
2. Verify IP SLA and track: show ip sla summary; show track.
3. Examine forwarding: show ip cef exact-route <src> <dst>.
4. Use debug ip policy with caution when needed.
Common Mistake

Applying PBR on the egress interface or forgetting a fallback next-hop are the fastest routes to create unreachable traffic. Always test with simulated failures before deploying to production.

screens.title: What is IP SLA?
screens.narratorSegment: IP Service Level Agreements provide active, programmable tests that a router runs to monitor reachability and performance of network paths. Unlike passive monitoring, IP SLA generates test traffic — for example ICMP echo, UDP echo, TCP connect, or HTTP requests — and measures metrics such as latency, jitter, and packet loss. An IP SLA operation is a single configured test; you schedule it and the router records results and statistics. You then create a track object that watches the IP SLA operation and reports a simple up/down state suitable for other features like route-maps. For instance, you might configure an ICMP echo to the primary next-hop every five seconds; if the operation starts failing, the associated track object moves to down and can trigger alternate forwarding. A misconception is that IP SLA is only for performance metrics; its most common operational use is simple reachability verification to make forwarding decisions safer. Remember to balance detection speed against noise — shorter intervals detect failures faster but increase probe traffic. The practical value is that IP SLA turns a static PBR into an adaptive one that responds to real path conditions automatically.

keyIdea.title: IP SLA purpose
keyIdea.text: IP SLA actively tests paths so network features can make forwarding decisions based on measured reachability and performance.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › What is IP SLA?
IP SLA basics
IP SLA runs active probes from a router to a target to measure reachability, latency, jitter, and packet loss. Each probe is an operation that can be scheduled and tracked.
Typical operations: ICMP echo for reachability, TCP connect for service checks, UDP jitter for voice QoS, and HTTP for application-level tests.
Track objects
A track object watches an IP SLA operation and exposes a boolean up/down state that other features can reference to make policy decisions.
Operational note
Select test frequency carefully. Excessive probing can create unnecessary control-plane load; choose intervals that balance detection time and stability.
Concrete scenario
Run an ICMP echo to 10.0.0.2 from the interface toward your primary ISP every five seconds. If replies stop, the linked track object flips to down and can trigger PBR to use a secondary next-hop.

screens.title: Configuring IP SLA and a Track Object
screens.narratorSegment: Configuring IP SLA begins by creating an operation and specifying what to test and from which interface. For example, ip sla 1 followed by icmp-echo 10.0.0.2 source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0 defines operation one as an ICMP echo to the primary next-hop using the specified source interface. Next, use frequency to set how often probes run and ip sla schedule to place the operation into the running schedule. After the operation is running, create a track object that monitors the operation's reachability with track 1 ip sla 1 reachability. That track object becomes a simple up/down signal other features can reference. A common misconception is to expect IP SLA results to automatically change routing — they do not. You must reference the track object from a route-map or a feature that supports tracking. Also be mindful of frequency: set it to detect failures quickly enough for your SLA targets but not so often that it burdens C P U and memory. Finally, use show ip sla summary and show track to confirm the operation status and the track object's state. Practice by configuring an operation and observing the transition when you shut down the primary interface.

keyIdea.title: Command flow
keyIdea.text: Define an IP SLA operation, schedule it, and create a track object to expose its state for use by other features.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › Configuring IP SLA
Config snippet
ip sla 1
 icmp-echo 10.0.0.2 source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 1 life forever start-time now
!
track 1 ip sla 1 reachability
This sequence creates operation 1, runs ICMP probes every five seconds, schedules it to run continuously, and tracks its reachability as track object one.
What to check
  • show ip sla summary — confirms operations and basic results.
  • show ip sla statistics <id> — detailed per-operation metrics.
  • show track — confirms track object is up or down based on the IP SLA.
Misconception
IP SLA alone does not change forwarding; link it to other features via track objects and route-maps for automated actions.

screens.title: Integrating IP SLA with PBR
screens.narratorSegment: Integrating IP SLA with PBR lets you make forwarding decisions based on measured path state. The essential step is to reference a track object from the route-map using set ip next-hop verify-availability. When the track object is up, the router will accept that set and forward matched traffic to the verified next-hop. If the track goes down, the route-map falls through to the next set statement, which can specify an alternate next-hop or allow the routing table to handle forwarding. This provides automated failover without human intervention. A concrete workflow: create an IP SLA operation testing the primary next-hop, schedule it, create a track object watching the SLA, then in your route-map use set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.0.0.2 1 followed by set ip next-hop 10.0.1.2. Apply the route-map inbound on the client-facing interface and test by bringing down the primary interface. The misconception to avoid is assuming verify-availability performs continuous redirects — it only controls whether that particular set is installed. Test and observe with show ip sla summary and show track to validate behavior and confirm the route-map fallthrough works as intended.

narration.text: Integrating IP SLA with PBR lets you make forwarding decisions based on measured path state. The essential step is to reference a track object from the route-map using set ip next-hop verify-availability. When the track object is up, the router will accept that set and forward matched traffic to the verified next-hop. If the track goes down, the route-map falls through to the next set statement, which can specify an alternate next-hop or allow the routing table to handle forwarding. This provides automated failover without human intervention. A concrete workflow: create an IP SLA operation testing the primary next-hop, schedule it, create a track object watching the SLA, then in your route-map use set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.0.0.2 1 followed by set ip next-hop 10.0.1.2. Apply the route-map inbound on the client-facing interface and test by bringing down the primary interface. The misconception to avoid is assuming verify-availability performs continuous redirects — it only controls whether that particular set is installed. Test and observe with show ip sla summary and show track to validate behavior and confirm the route-map fallthrough works as intended.

Route-map example

keyIdea.text: A single, consistent configuration ties ACLs, route-map, IP SLA, and track objects together to provide monitored, policy-driven failover.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 1.6 › R1 Full Config
Router R1 configuration (example)
hostname R1
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ip address 10.0.0.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/1
 ip address 10.0.1.1 255.255.255.0
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 ip address 192.168.10.1 255.255.255.0
!
access-list 101 permit ip 192.168.10.0 0.0.0.255 any
!
ip sla 1
 icmp-echo 10.0.0.2 source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 frequency 5
ip sla schedule 1 life forever start-time now
!
track 1 ip sla 1 reachability
!
route-map PBR_PRIMARY permit 10
 match ip address 101
 set ip next-hop verify-availability 10.0.0.2 1
 set ip next-hop 10.0.1.2
!
interface GigabitEthernet0/2
 ip policy route-map PBR_PRIMARY
This complete example creates the necessary ACL, IP SLA, track object, route-map with a verified next-hop and fallback, and applies the policy on the interface where client traffic enters R1.

screens.title: Verification and Troubleshooting
screens.narratorSegment: After configuring PBR and IP SLA, verification is crucial. Start with show ip policy to confirm the route-map is bound to the expected interface. Use show ip sla summary to verify the operation is running and to see recent statistics. Check show track to confirm the track object's state is up; this tells you whether verify-availability will permit the primary next-hop. To observe actual forwarding for a specific flow, use show ip cef exact-route with a source and destination to see which next-hop CEF chooses for that packet. When the track goes down, re-run the exact-route command to confirm traffic now uses the secondary path. For packet-level testing, ping from the client subnet with a specified source to simulate real traffic and verify paths. If something doesn't behave as expected, check ACL matches and route-map ordering, and ensure you applied the policy inbound on the correct interface. Use debug ip policy cautiously for live troubleshooting. A common diagnostic step is to administratively shut the primary link to observe track flipping and to confirm the route-map falls through to the intended secondary set. These commands give you both the state and the evidence of traffic steering working correctly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn how Policy-Based Routing lets you direct traffic using rules other than the normal destination-based lookup, and how IP SLA adds active measurements so those rules can respond to real-time path conditions. We'll ground the theory in common enterprise use cases: offloading application flows to a particular ISP, forcing traffic through a firewall, and implementing automatic failover when a primary link fails. You'll see the core building blocks: access lists to match traffic, route-maps to express actions, and IP SLA operations plus track objects to monitor reachability. A concrete example will walk through configuring a router with two internet paths and steering traffic from a subnet to the preferred next-hop, with IP SLA verifying availability and failing over to the backup. Also pay attention to the common mistakes: applying PBR on the wrong interface, misunderstanding directionality, or forgetting fallbacks. By the end you'll know not only how to write the commands, but how to test, verify, and reason about behavior under failure. Consider the question: when would you prefer PBR over policy in a routing protocol, and what monitoring interval would you choose for a business-critical application?

By the end of this first objectives page you will be able to explain when and why Policy-Based Routing is useful, and you will be able to configure PBR to forward traffic based on criteria other than destination. Specifically, you will learn how access lists define the traffic to match and how route-maps express the forwarding action. You'll see examples where source-based steering sends a subnet to a particular next-hop to meet business policy, and we'll contrast that with standard routing so you can predict effects on return paths. You'll also begin to configure IP SLA operations to monitor reachability, including choosing an appropriate test type like ICMP echo for simple reachability checks or TCP connect for service-aware monitoring. Each objective focuses on practical configuration and why the step matters in real networks. Pay attention to directionality: PBR applies to traffic entering an interface, which is a frequent source of mistakes. As you work through the lab steps, ask: which traffic should be matched, and how will return traffic behave once we force a specific next-hop?

On this second page of objectives we focus on the integration, verification, and operational best practices that make PBR and IP SLA production-ready. You will implement IP SLA tracking and tie tracked state to route-map actions using the set ip next-hop verify-availability command so policy decisions depend on measured reachability. You will learn verification and troubleshooting commands—show ip policy, show ip sla summary, show track, and show ip cef exact-route—to confirm behavior and to observe how traffic moves under normal and failure conditions. Safety and operational notes are also objectives: choose reasonable IP SLA frequencies to avoid excessive control-plane traffic and always provide a fallback next-hop or allow the routing table to take over to avoid black holes. Lastly, you'll practice a hands-on scenario that configures R1 with both primary and secondary next-hops, exercises failover by shutting down an interface, and observes track state change. These are the operational skills that let you deploy PBR+IP SLA with confidence in a live network.

Policy-Based Routing is a method to forward packets according to rules you define, instead of relying exclusively on the routing table's destination-based decision. In practice, you match traffic — often using an access list — and then set a forwarding action in a route-map. The motivation is straightforward: enterprise networks often need traffic steering that reflects business needs rather than pure topology. For example, you might force all voice traffic through a low-latency WAN link, or route traffic from a particular branch through a security appliance for inspection. PBR is also used for load sharing between two internet providers by steering different subnets to different next-hops. A common misconception is that PBR changes how return traffic is routed; it only affects the router where the policy is evaluated. That makes thinking about symmetric flows important: if you force outbound traffic to a different path, the return path might not return via the same device unless you design the network for it. As a takeaway, PBR is powerful for granular control, but you must plan matching criteria, return path symmetry, and fallbacks to avoid creating black holes.

PBR configuration follows a disciplined process with four core steps, and understanding each step helps you design safe policies. Step one is defining what traffic to match, typically with a standard or extended access-list that identifies source subnets, destination networks, protocol type, or ports. Step two is creating a route-map entry that uses match ip address to reference that access-list. Step three is defining the action with set commands: set ip next-hop to select a specific next-hop IP, or set interface to send traffic out a chosen interface. There is also verify-availability to consult a track object from IP SLA. The final step is applying the route-map to an ingress interface using ip policy route-map. A common error is applying the policy to the wrong interface or in the wrong direction; the router evaluates PBR only on traffic entering the interface where you applied the policy. Another important operational point is the order of set commands in a route-map: when you include verify-availability the router uses the tracked state to decide whether that set is valid and then falls through to subsequent sets. As an exercise, write the access-list, reference it from a route-map with permit 10, and apply ip policy on the client-facing interface. This disciplined sequence reduces misconfiguration and makes troubleshooting straightforward.

Normal routing uses destination IP and the longest-prefix match rule to choose the outgoing interface and next-hop. That model is simple, scalable, and works for the vast majority of traffic. Policy-Based Routing is an intentional exception to that model: you introduce business-driven rules that can override the routing table for selected flows. Use PBR when you need deterministic steering based on source, protocol, or application rather than the destination. A classic use case is sending a subnet to a specific ISP for contractual or performance reasons, or directing application traffic through a security appliance for inspection. However, PBR adds operational complexity: policies are processed before the normal route lookup completes, and they only affect traffic processed by the router where the policy is applied. A common misunderstanding is to assume PBR will rewrite return traffic paths; in reality, PBR affects only the router performing the match. If two devices apply asymmetric PBRs you can create forwarding loops or drops, so test for symmetry and include fallback behaviors. In general, reserve PBR for flows that need special handling and prefer routing protocol solutions for broad reachability and dynamic path selection unless policy-level steering is required.

Several mistakes recur when engineers implement PBR, and anticipating them saves time in deployment. First, applying the route-map on the wrong interface or in the wrong direction is the most common error. Remember, ip policy route-map is evaluated on traffic entering the interface, so apply it on the interface facing the traffic source. Second, administrators forget that PBR does not affect traffic the router itself originates; locally-generated packets are not evaluated by an interface policy unless you configure ip local policy route-map. Third, missing fallbacks can create black holes. Always include a secondary set ip next-hop or allow the route-map to fall through so the routing table can handle traffic if policy paths fail. Fourth, order matters: verify-availability is evaluated in the order of set statements in the route-map; if the verified next-hop is down, PBR falls through to the next set. Finally, excessive IP SLA frequency can overload control plane processing. Use conservative frequencies and balance detection speed with stability. When troubleshooting, show ip policy and show track will quickly reveal whether the policy is applied and whether the tracked object is up or down. Ask yourself: have I accounted for the router's locally-originated traffic and provided safe fallbacks?

IP Service Level Agreements provide active, programmable tests that a router runs to monitor reachability and performance of network paths. Unlike passive monitoring, IP SLA generates test traffic — for example ICMP echo, UDP echo, TCP connect, or HTTP requests — and measures metrics such as latency, jitter, and packet loss. An IP SLA operation is a single configured test; you schedule it and the router records results and statistics. You then create a track object that watches the IP SLA operation and reports a simple up/down state suitable for other features like route-maps. For instance, you might configure an ICMP echo to the primary next-hop every five seconds; if the operation starts failing, the associated track object moves to down and can trigger alternate forwarding. A misconception is that IP SLA is only for performance metrics; its most common operational use is simple reachability verification to make forwarding decisions safer. Remember to balance detection speed against noise — shorter intervals detect failures faster but increase probe traffic. The practical value is that IP SLA turns a static PBR into an adaptive one that responds to real path conditions automatically.

Configuring IP SLA begins by creating an operation and specifying what to test and from which interface. For example, ip sla 1 followed by icmp-echo 10.0.0.2 source-interface GigabitEthernet0/0 defines operation one as an ICMP echo to the primary next-hop using the specified source interface. Next, use frequency to set how often probes run and ip sla schedule to place the operation into the running schedule. After the operation is running, create a track object that monitors the operation's reachability with track 1 ip sla 1 reachability. That track object becomes a simple up/down signal other features can reference. A common misconception is to expect IP SLA results to automatically change routing — they do not. You must reference the track object from a route-map or a feature that supports tracking. Also be mindful of frequency: set it to detect failures quickly enough for your SLA targets but not so often that it burdens C P U and memory. Finally, use show ip sla summary and show track to confirm the operation status and the track object's state. Practice by configuring an operation and observing the transition when you shut down the primary interface.

Here are the fundamental concepts you should retain. Policy-Based Routing allows forwarding decisions based on criteria other than destination — for example, source IP, protocol, or port — using access lists and route-maps. A route-map is the configuration vehicle that matches traffic and specifies actions such as set ip next-hop or set interface; its sequence numbers and ordering matter, especially when multiple set statements are present. IP SLA is the active monitoring feature that probes a target to measure reachability or performance; you schedule operations and review their statistics. Together, these tools let you implement intelligent, policy-driven traffic steering that can react to measured path conditions. Keep in mind operational cautions: apply policies on the ingress interface, include fallbacks, and choose IP SLA intervals that balance detection speed with control-plane load. Now, consider how you'd combine these concepts in your next topology to keep critical traffic on preferred paths while remaining resilient to link failures.

These final concept cards reinforce operational points to carry into labs and production. An IP SLA operation is a specific test such as ICMP echo or TCP connect that the router uses to judge a remote target's availability. A track object watches that operation and reports a simple up or down state that can be referenced from route-maps or other features. Dynamic path selection is the combined behavior where PBR consults a tracked IP SLA result and automatically prefers a verified next-hop or falls back to a secondary path. In practice, design your policies with fallbacks, test for asymmetric routing, and choose probe frequencies that meet detection targets without overwhelming device resources. Practice the lab scenario, verify with show commands, and consider the business requirement behind each steering decision. Ask yourself: does the policy improve availability or create unnecessary complexity? That question will guide safe and maintainable deployments.
